ABSTRACT Leak rates of methane (CH4) from the natural gas supply chain result in lost profit from unsold product, public safety and property concerns due to potential explosion hazards, and a potentially large source of economic damages from legal liabilities. Yet large measurement challenges exist in identifying and quantifying CH4 leak rates along the vast number and type of components in the natural gas supply chain. This is particularly true of the “midstream” components involved in the gathering, processing, compression, transmission, and storage of natural gas. This project developed and deployed new advances in chirped laser dispersion spectroscopy (CLaDS) to detect methane leaks from pipelines, compressor stations, and other midstream infrastructure from a remote position (standoff detection). The system was deployed from a van to measure fugitive methane leaks from a local compressor station as a proof-of-concept. The technique was validated through mobile laboratory measurements with in-situ sensors as well as controlled releases of methane. The system also mapped a plume from a controlled release of methane by tracking a small unmanned aerial system (sUAS) that carried a corner cube retroreflector which reflected the beam back to the instrument. The drone-based system quantified a leak rate to within 30% of the actual rate and localized the emission location within 5 m of the actual release location at standoff distances of 25-45 m. This sUAS-reflector tracking approach has benefits for mapping leak locations remotely using small drones flying around a facility. Benefits of a commercial sensor with these capabilities include reductions of leaks for pipeline operators (more profit), earlier detection of leaks to avoid catastrophic explosion hazards for public health and to mitigate property damage, and reduced methane emissions to the atmosphere (improving air quality).

SUMMARY OF PROJECT ACTIVITIES Task 1.0 – Project management and planning Status: Completed. The project management plan (PMP) was submitted within 30 days of the award. Task 2.0 – Development of HE‐CM‐CLaDS sensor Status: Completed. The objective of this task was to develop a heterodyne enhanced chirp modulated chirped laser absorption spectroscopy (HE‐CM‐CLaDS) system for remote methane detection. Specifically, this task focused on implementation of the heterodyne‐enhancement to improve back-scatter signal as well as development of range‐finding capabilities.

The system had been fully developed by February 2018 according to the diagram in Figure 1 and configured as a transportable instrument as shown in Figure 2. The system could seamlessly switch between conventional CLaDS and HE-CLaDS operation modes used for specular reflection targets with received optical power > 10 µW and for diffuse reflection targets returning < 10 µW respectively. The range-finding capability was also developed and successfully implemented into the instrument’s routine measurement procedure. Task 3.0 – Laboratory testing of system parameters Status: Completed. In this task, the system developed under Task 2.0 was fully tested and its performance in terms of methane sensitivity, instrument drift, heterodyne‐enhancement, and range‐finding performance was evaluated according to a Laboratory Test Plan submitted to the DOE. Different target materials were also tested to determine the system limitations in hard‐target remote sensing schemes. The test results performed in both a well-controlled fiber-coupled test configuration as well as in the target free-space configuration are summarized in Table 1 below.

*Table 1. The general system performance met the originally proposed milestones which included a path-integrated concentration sensitivity of < 1 ppmv⋅m⋅Hz-1/2 CH4 in atmospheric air, range-finding resolution of < 0.1 m, and optical heterodyne enhancement of > 10 dB as compared to direct CLaDS. Task 4.0 – Outdoor testing and validation of sensor performance Status: Completed. This task was designed to demonstrate the performance of the system outside in a field environment with the goals of quantifying precision, accuracy, and range resolution. There were two sub-tasks: 4.1) focused on the development of a 100 m round‐trip outdoor calibration system, and 4.2) focused on calibration of sensor precision, accuracy, and resolution using different backscattering targets. A calibration facility was developed comprising of a 5 m long polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipe (used as a large gas cell) that was placed 50 meters away from the system. The pipe was equipped with a polycarbonate sheet window, a back plate used to mount different reflecting targets, and a gas handling system used to test different CH4 gas mixtures. A commercial point sensor (LI-7700) was also used inside the PVC pipe as a reference sensor. As a result of the tests, the HE-CLaDS instrument showed excellent ability to clearly distinguish path-averaged CH4 concentrations 0 to 8 ppmv above the ~2 ppmv atmospheric background over effective target reflectivities spanning three orders of magnitude from 10% to 0.01% (see Figure 3). This represented a successful accomplishment of both sub-tasks with all system parameters within the anticipated Decision Point #1 success criteria.*

The measured concentrations showed excellent agreement with predicted values estimated based on reference sensor calibration. Task 5.0 – Development of tomographic reconstruction algorithms Status: Completed. The Horizontal Radial Plume Mapping (HRPM) technique was used for the development of tomographic reconstruction algorithms. Our methodology was adapted from one developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) (Hashmonay et al., 2008) for open-path, pathintegrated optical remote sensing systems. HRPM is designed to locate sources of fugitive emissions close to the ground. To evaluate our implementation of HRPM we collected measurements from 16 retroreflectors over a 2500 square meter area in an empty field on the Princeton University campus. In particular, our experiments used a 4x4 grid with a grid spacing of 12.5 m, and the CLaDS system was placed 25 meters below the edge of the grid to demonstrate the accuracy of the ranging capabilities of CLaDS (in this case up to 80 m away). This is represented schematically in Figure 4. The system was able to switch between retroreflectors in approximately two seconds. The system locked on to retroreflectors using a centroid tracking algorithm in order to optimize the power received at the detector. The signal was averaged for durations between 20-60 s per position. Full sweeps of the grid used for tomographic reconstruction spanned 6 to 16 minutes.*

After successfully implementing this technique, we were able to compare field-based rangeresolved CH4 concentrations measured by CLaDS with modeled concentrations using a Gaussian plume model as the forward model. An inverse Gaussian approach was used to make leak rate estimations. Results for this are presented in Task 7.0 where we extended our measurement capability from a stationary grid of retroreflectors to a retroreflector mounted on a flying drone. A mass balance approach was not investigated because of the cancellation of manned aircraft flights due to social distancing measures and lockdowns as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic (see Task 8.0). Task 6.0 – Mobile field tests Status: Completed. The CLaDS system was deployed for a series of outdoor measurements of methane emissions. The CLaDS instrument was transported in a rented van and remained in the vehicle during the measurements. Two types of field tests were performed: 1) controlled release measurements at an empty field in Princeton, and 2) monitoring of natural gas leaks from a compressor station in central New Jersey (the setup is shown in Figure 5a). In both tests, to validate the CLaDS instrument performance, a mobile laboratory equipped with a CH4 point-sensor (LI-7700) was also deployed in the field for reference measurements. An example sub-set of data collected at the compressor station is shown in Figure 5b. Excellent agreement between the CLaDS data and the mobile lab data was observed, and the tests clearly indicated that stand-off detection measurements with multiple retroreflectors (multiple optical beam paths), or with a drone-based reflector target providing large-area coverage, could potentially be used for more accurate plume localization. The drone-based detection scheme was studied in detail for Task 7.0.

*Figure 5. (a) Google Maps screenshot showing the location of the instrument and two retroreflectors establishing two beam paths north of the transmission station. (b) raw data (top) and 10-second averaged values (bottom) of the CH4 concentrations measured by the CLaDS instrument compared with those measured by the mobile lab point-sensor as the mobile lab drove through the beam path of the CLaDS instrument. Task 7.0 – Drone-based reflector target imaging Status: Completed. One of the major goals of this project was to develop and test a micro-drone (hand-sized, ~200 g) open-path sensing system capable of measuring spatial profiles of CH4 plumes. In order to*

accomplish this goal, we implemented a path-integrated concentration measurement system leveraging an airborne, sUAS-mounted retroreflector to provide a novel open-path sensing modality for CH4 plume localization. The retroreflector relaxed constraints that otherwise would have been imposed by the positional imprecision of the sUAS flights by significantly reducing the dependence of the return signal on the orientation of the sUAS. After successful tests with the sUAS-mounted retroreflector, we developed tracking hardware and software to follow the sUAS along arbitrary paths to sample the spatial extent of methane plumes. Subtask 7.1 Develop tracking system for drone Initial attempts were focused on using a visible camera to measure the aiming error signal used to control a gimbal which angled the laser from the CLaDS system toward the sUAS-mounted retroreflector. This had limited success, as the camera frame rate was too low to successfully track a drone and maintain sufficiently high return signal power. Furthermore, the field of view was too small. A new approach studied under this project utilized an analog quadrant detector that was faster (bandwidth of 150 kHz) and enabled the system to track speeds and accelerations that were much higher bandwidth and even exceeding the bandwidth of the gimbal tracking system. This method was used in the field. Figure 6 shows a schematic and photos of the most recent versions of the CLaDS and drone tracking systems.

*Figure 6. Schematic and photos of CLaDS (red rectangle) and drone tracking systems. The photos show the CLaDS system locked onto the drone (DJI Mavic Mini) as well as the systems operating out of the back of a van. LD = laser diode, OI = optical isolator, FC = optical fiber coupler, GC = reference gas cell (filled with calibrated amounts of CH4), PD = photodetector, EOM = electro-optic modulator, C = collimator, OAP = off-axis parabolic mirror, GM = gimbal mirror, BS = beam splitter, QPD = quadrant photodetector Compared to previous iterations, the systems were simplified without sacrificing performance so that they were more portable and easier to deploy in outdoor field environments. A key change was to use the IR laser for both methane sensing with a fast photodetector (PD3) and drone tracking with a quadrant photodetector (QPD). Previously, the system relied on a visible red alignment laser for tracking. During experiments when sunlight was strong, the red light of the sunlight spectrum interfered with the silicon QPD meant for the red alignment laser. Replacing the silicon QPD with*

a QPD only sensitive to infrared light and redesigning the system as shown in Figure 6 solved the problem. The redesign also led to fewer components in the transmitter of the system, increasing the launch efficiency of the system. We have extended the field-deployability of the system; the drone can now be tracked when there is strong sunlight background (even with bright objects within the field of view). One of the limitations of the current technique is that it does not use a large quadrant detector, and therefore the effective field is still smaller than ideal. Further improvements for the tracking algorithm are discussed in Task 8.0. Subtask 7.2 Conduct flight tests Figure 7 shows an aerial view of the setup on the Princeton University campus. A gas cylinder of 99.9% methane was used for controlled release experiments. In addition, we used an electric vehicle equipped with a LICOR LI-7700 methane point sensor to collect data for comparison with CLaDS. Finally, to discern in-flight performance, we placed a 2" retroreflector on a tripod at fixed downwind distances to compare with the drone-based retroreflector at nearly the same positions.

*Figure 7. Overview of the drone-based testing as observed from a photo taken by the drone (left). Photos of test flights with drone (DJI Phantom 4) and mounted retro-reflector (right). A more compact and lightweight drone (DJI Mavic Mini) was used for Subtask 7.3. Subtask 7.3 Image controlled release plume Path-integrated concentration and simultaneous ranging measurements from CLaDS in addition to micrometeorological measurements (3D wind, temperature, humidity) were used to construct images of CH4 plumes from the controlled release. Figure 8 shows the layout of the controlled release experiments for Subtask 7.3. The visual shape of enhancements of CH4 above ambient background, individual transects of CH4 plumes, and a stacked wall of transects downstream of the plume are also shown in Figure 8. The mass-balance method was proposed with manned aircraft flights in mind, but these were cancelled due to the pandemic. The system was able to track the drone up to a height of 8 meters (26 ft), 16.5 meters from the van (i.e., vertical field of view of 26 degrees), but instead, we focused on high-resolution, real-time plume mapping, which consisted of 2D horizontal flights. The horizontal field of view of the system was 75 degrees. Tomographic reconstruction algorithms developed for Task 5.0 were used with inverse Gaussian models to estimate the source location as if the location was unknown. These results are shown in Figure 9.*

*Figure 8. Experimental setup with points of interest plotted using the Google Maps API. The circles with the blue-toyellow color scale show combined data for two 40-minute sweeps of a controlled CH4 plume. The bottom-right inset shows a histogram of the wind data collected from the micrometeorology tower for the duration of the two sweeps. Ambient background CH4 concentrations were measured with a LICOR LI-7810 trace gas analyzer upwind of the release point. A second LI-7810 was placed right next to the van. In these experiments, the drone (Mavic Mini) was flown away from the system in a linear fashion, starting 25 meters away and ending 40 meters from the system, at six different distances and angular sweeps referenced to the van. This pattern was designed to provide maximal spatial coverage while taking into account the battery life of the sUAS and allowing for battery swaps between linear scans. Over the course of 1 hour, we collected measurements along 6 linear paths at 6 distances along each path, providing an effective grid of 36 points with dwell times of 30-60 seconds at each point. During these dwell times, concentration retrievals were accurate for only about 60% of the dwell time due to rapid drone accelerations caused by gusty wind conditions, as well as some turbulence. Spectroscopic data were collected in real time, and the ranging measurements were defined by the distance-dependent frequency shift induced by chirped modulation of the signal sidebands (see Task 2.0 and Task 3.0). To track the target, the quadrant detector was used in a PII2 control loop with the motorized gimbal to track the position of the retroreflector, as described in Subtask 7.1. We were able to track the drone even with gusts of wind with speeds up to 10 m⋅s-1. Additionally, the system performed well without additional mechanical stabilization of the instrument van; additional jack supports were not required, unlike most optical instrumentation which tend to be very sensitive to physical perturbations.*

*Figure 9 shows estimated source locations based on minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between the measurements in Figure 8 and modeled concentrations derived from a Gaussian plume model with total reflection off the ground. Inputs to the model included a controlled leak rate of methane of 24.3 L⋅min-1, mean wind speed of 3.5 ± 1 m⋅s-1, and release height of 1.5 meters. We approximated the height of the drone as 1.5 meters. The hovering accuracy of the drone was 0.1 meters, but the absolute accuracy of the height of the drone was approximately 1 meter. Wind direction and other micrometeorological data were acquired from METEK uSonic-3 Class A (3D wind, temperature), LICOR LI-7500 (humidity, H2O), and LI-7700 (10 Hz CH4) sensors mounted on a tripodal tower. Figure 9 shows best fits of the source location for two sets of data. The first column of plots shows coarse estimations of location with 1 meter grid spacing, while the second column shows optimal locations and inverse mean square errors for finer grid spacing. The final column provides approximate locations of the source, overlaid on the mean sUAS locations, which are derived from the raw sUAS locations shown in Figure 8.*

*Figure 9. Source localization and leak rate estimation. An approximate location is first found with a coarse sweep at 1 meter resolution. The optimal location is denoted by the red circle. The axis from 30 to 10 shows the N/S distance from the van in meters. The axis from -10 to 5 shows the E/W distance from the van in meters. After finding an approximate location, a finer resolution scan in the vicinity of the estimated optimal location was performed, as shown in the second column. This was done for a number of potential flow rates, between 10 and 40 L⋅min-1. The final column shows CLaDS measurements overlaid on the plume as computed from the Gaussian plume model. The estimated flow rates are 24 and 14 L⋅min-1 for the top and bottom graphs respectively (actual = 24.3 L⋅min-1). The color axis is plotted on a log scale and corresponds to path-integrated CH4 concentrations for the CLaDS measurements and point concentrations for the modeled plume. The data in Figure 9 show that the approximate source location agrees within 1 meter of error between the two experiments, showcasing the ability of the system to accurately estimate the source location between two sets of measurements, given a controlled release rate of CH4. The method was also repeatable because the two sets of data were taken approximately an hour apart, when the mean wind speed and direction were different. Varying meteorological parameters were taken into account by the model. The modeled source location is within the uncertainty range of 5 meters, arising in part from relative errors in the GPS data for the drone and vehicle at short*

distances (± 2 m). The estimated emission rates were within uncertainty ranges of 30% and showed good agreement with emission rates derived from the point sensor (LI-7700) mounted on top of an electrical vehicle (shown in Figure 7) that was sampling the plume downwind of the source. 30% is also the uncertainty range derived from measurements using the LI-7700. The source localization method is also being tested on data from unknown leak rates from a compressor station in New Jersey. These analyses were not completed in time for the final report, but these results are currently in review in an academic journal (Optics Letters). Task 8.0 – Airborne flight measurements Status: Cancelled. Subtask 8.1 Integrate system onto aircraft For aircraft flights and faster drone flights, the tracking system was improved such that it could handle faster motion. We had been developing a hybrid approach integrating the fast tracking of s quadrant detector with the slower tracking capability of a visible light camera, in a multicomponent feedback loop to maintain tracking during increased flight velocities. (See Subtask 7.1). Scattered signal collection efficiency utilizing the current telescope design was too low due to limited telescope aperture. Additionally, development began on a novel narrow-linewidth laser fiber amplifier to increase the power of the laser output power by a few orders of magnitude, thereby increasing the scattered signal collected by the system. When used in conjunction with HE-CLaDS, we anticipate a significant improvement in methane sensing capability at long distances and with poor quality reflective surfaces. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic and associated social distancing safety protocols, manned aircraft flights were cancelled and as per the 2021 revised statement of project objectives (SOPO); the rest of Task 8.0 was cancelled. CONCLUSIONS & IMPLICATIONS We demonstrated that an open-path laser spectrometer and a drone carrying a retroreflector can be used to make maps of plumes and localize sources of CH4 emissions. Comparisons with a two separate controlled release experiments showed location accuracy of 5 m and emission rate accuracy of ± 30%. The technology developed in this project is not only limited to methane. We could use the same techniques with different lasers in a similar architecture to measure other chemical species. Additionally, we demonstrated the simultaneous ranging capability of CLaDS, which other spectroscopic techniques do not have. Simultaneous ranging was especially useful for drone measurements where optical pathlength is highly variable. We developed a real-time system for actively tracking the drone during flight. Many technical advancements were needed to overcome unexpected hurdles during the course of this project, due to a lack of commercially available drone tracking solutions. With our results, we have provided evidence that it is technologically feasible to perform open-path standoff detection with unmanned


<!-- Page 14 -->


13

aerial systems. The drone tracking system we have developed can serve as a platform for further technological advancements in field-deployable, open-path gas sensing. With higher optical power, CLaDS could work for not only drones but also manned aircraft missions. Higher power would also result in sufficiently high backscattered signal, in which case retroreflectors and therefore strict pointing requirements would not be necessary. The range of options for reflective elements could be extended to include the surfaces of commonly-used equipment and prevalent natural features. However, experimental results for this have not yet been demonstrated. Narrow-linewidth Raman fiber laser amplifiers are one potential solution that we believe is worth pursuing in the future.
